tfcpp.info.basic_brick: Burnt dolomite pressed with coal tar, and not fired. Eight of them in an empty converter make its lining basic, and repair a basic lining as fire bricks repair an acid one.
tfcpp.info.borosilicate_glass_batch: Sand, lime and borax. Load it into a blowpipe and work it as any batch: this is the glass that stands heat and acid. Makes the glass carboy and the glass retort.
tfcpp.info.coal: Coal seams hold methane, more of it the deeper they lie, and some rock next to them holds gas under pressure. Mining lets it out. A flame lights air holding 5% to 15% of it, and the blast is followed by afterdamp full of carbon monoxide.
tfcpp.info.coke_oven: A closed chamber of fire brick, heated from below, that distils a charge of up to 64 pieces of coal or wood without air. Its gas goes up the pipe above it, or into the room if there is no pipe, its tar and liquor condense in the tanks of a condenser beside it, and the coke is taken out when the batch is done. Without a condenser the tar and liquor are lost as vapour, and the gas is poisonous, so lead it into a pipe.
tfcpp.info.condensation_tower: Put it in a run of pipe that carries furnace fumes. While the gas is below 250 C, arsenic, antimony, zinc and lead oxide settle on its walls as dust, and mercury runs down as a liquid when the gas is below 100 C. Sulfur dioxide goes on through. Scrape the dust off with an empty hand while crouching, which stirs some of it into the air, and tap the mercury into a container. Several towers in a row catch proportionally more.
tfcpp.info.converter: Set below a blast furnace or pour in molten iron, then blow air through it from a pipe at a pressure above about 1.7 atm. Silicon burns first in a shower of sparks, then carbon in a long flame, and when the flame drops the iron itself starts to burn. Stop while the flame is shortening for steel. No fuel is used: the reactions alone keep the iron liquid, but only with a strong enough blast, and iron that sets in the vessel stops the blow. Water in the pipe will blow it apart. Reline it with fire bricks when it is empty. A new vessel is lined with silica, and phosphorus stays in the iron: a tap of it is brittle cold short iron. Eight basic bricks laid in an empty vessel make the lining basic. Throw lime powder into a basic vessel, and after the carbon is gone the phosphorus burns out as thick white smoke into Thomas slag, if there is lime enough for the silicon and the phosphorus both. The silica of a basic vessel with no lime eats its lining.
tfcpp.info.cupel_hearth: A fire-brick hearth floored with bone ash, over a fire. Pour in work lead and blow air over it: the lead oxidises to litharge, which is raked off, and the silver is left to be tapped at the end. Keep the hearth hot enough for the litharge to stay liquid, and do not breathe the lead fume that the blast raises.
tfcpp.info.davy_lamp: A lamp whose gauze keeps its flame from lighting the air around it. Carried in hand with oil in it, it shows firedamp as a blue cap above the flame, and goes out when oxygen runs low, or when the firedamp is thick enough to starve it. A flame that has gone out stays out until you light it again with flint and steel from the other hand (or with a lighter, if the lamp is standing). It does not show carbon monoxide, and a gauze with gas burning in it for minutes gets hot enough to light the gas outside.
tfcpp.info.gas_burner: A nozzle with a hand wheel that burns the gas of the pipe it is joined to, under whatever stands on it. Light it with flint and steel or a fire starter: a lit burner is an open flame to any gas in the room, so do not open it near methane or coal gas.
tfcpp.info.glass_carboy: Holds 25 L of acids, the chemical liquids of the mod, vinegar and fresh water, and nothing else. Right-click a tank or a retort to pour or draw.
tfcpp.info.glass_retort: Set it over a sand bath, with a retort condenser beside it. Right-click with a carboy to pour in the liquids (a recipe takes one or two) and water for the receiver, or powder into the slot. Heat it only to the working range of the charge: nothing comes over below it, and glass cracks above 550 C, spilling everything. Without a condenser the acids escape as fumes, and without water in the receiver hydrogen chloride goes into the air. Crouch with a carboy to draw off the flask's own liquids, and with an empty hand to take out the powder, both what the batches left and what no batch has taken. The last film under a litre cannot be poured out of the flask: crouching with the carboy rinses it onto the floor as fumes. Water can be piped into the receiver from any side. Chamber acid is concentrated by boiling its water off, so the strong acid stays in the flask, to be drawn from the bottom, and that needs no condenser.
tfcpp.info.gold_leaf_indicator: A leaf of gold on a thin plate, which mercury vapour whitens for good: from bright gold, through pale, to white. Place it where mercury may reach it, and read its stage with an empty hand; it shows no number. A leaf that has whitened comes up as nothing when it is broken, and a clean one comes up as a new leaf.
tfcpp.info.iron_slag: Holds iron that the furnace could not get out. It melts back into a blast furnace or bloomery charge.
tfcpp.info.lead_chamber: A chamber of lead sheet in a pipe run, where sulfur dioxide, air, steam and the oxides of nitrogen make chamber acid on its walls. Lead holds the acid while it is cool, so the tank can be drawn off into a carboy by hand. The oxides of nitrogen are poisonous, and they leak out of any joint that is not sealed. The lead wears under the acid in its tank, in proportion to how full the tank is, and above 80 C the film of sulfate that protects it dissolves and it wears twenty times faster: keep the gas cool and draw the tank off.
tfcpp.info.manometer: Right-click to read the pressure. Above 3 atm over the air outside the mercury is blown out of the tube, into the room, once. The tube then leaks a hundredth of the bore, and the pipes keep their pressure otherwise.
tfcpp.info.marsh_apparatus: Charge it with a millibucket of sulfuric or chamber acid from a carboy in the other hand, which gives eight tests. Right-click in the air to test the air at your eye, or with a sample in the other hand: white arsenic, antimony oxide, tetrahedrite ore or arsenical copper. A mirror says that arsenic or antimony is there, and not which one; the arsine it makes is poisonous, so test in the open.
tfcpp.info.mine_fan: Driven by a shaft at its back, it blows out of its front and draws air in through its other sides, along the open spaces leading to it. Air moves quickly along a narrow drift and hardly at all across a large chamber. It only moves air that has somewhere to come from: in a dead end or a room with no other opening to the sky it does nothing but stir, and the second shaft is what makes a working ventilable. Right-click it to see what it found. The fan loads the shaft more the faster it turns.
tfcpp.info.phosphoric_iron_slag: Slag from smelting brown ore, as rich in phosphorus as the tap cinder of a real bloomery. It melts back as phosphoric oxide, so it does not clean anything.
tfcpp.info.pipes: A run of pipe is one volume at one pressure, and bursts at its weakest wall or joint. Hemp and tallow joints hold 10 atm at most. Corrosion thins the walls: copper suffers from ammonia and mercury, iron from brine and chlorine, and wood chars when hot. Breaking a pipe lets out everything in the run, so close a valve first. Two different liquids never join: pipes that carry them touch without opening to each other, and a pipe put between them takes the side whose liquid comes first in the alphabet. Liquid weighs: a tall column presses on its foot with 1 atm for every 10 m of water, and that pressure is added to what the lowest joint must hold. Hot water in a boiler that bursts flashes to steam at once, adds its energy to the blast and scalds everyone within four blocks. A pipe whose wall is gone by more than a twentieth gives nothing back when it is broken. Valves, vents, taps and safety valves are made in iron, lead and fired clay, and take the wall strength and the corrosion of their body, as pipes do. Fired clay (chemical stoneware) stands every strong acid at any heat, but it is brittle and holds only 3.5 atm, and hot lye takes its glaze. Lead stands chamber acid below 80 C, nitric acid eats it, and it holds 5.9 atm. A valve of iron in an acid line lasts hours or days.
tfcpp.info.piston_pump: Driven by a shaft from the side. It takes in from the back, from a pipe, a barrel, standing water or the air, and delivers into a pipe at the front. Every turn sweeps the same volume, and the shaft pays for the difference in pressure and for lifting the liquid to the height of its surface in the pipe in front. The atmosphere pushes water up a suction pipe by 10.3 m at most, so a pump cannot draw from deeper. It does not take lava or molten metal, and it does not deliver into a line that runs on past loaded land. Right-click it to see which.
tfcpp.info.pressure_vessel: Half a cubic metre that joins any pipe touching it. A fire below heats everything in its network. Gas gains pressure in proportion to its absolute temperature, water adds its vapour pressure, and a vessel full of liquid with no room to expand gives way almost at once. Fit a safety valve.
tfcpp.info.safety_valve: An iron one lifts at 8 atm above the air outside and seats again at 7, with a loud hiss. It cannot be held shut. A lead or fired clay body holds less, so its weight is set to four fifths of what the body holds: about 4.7 atm for lead and 2.8 for fired clay, with the seat 1 atm lower.
tfcpp.info.sand_bath: A tray of sand between a fire and glass. It passes up only 20 C plus a share of the fire's excess over that, one part in the depth plus one, so deeper sand gives a cooler vessel. Empty hand adds a layer, crouching removes one.
tfcpp.info.sentinel_cage: Right-click a rat or a quail with an empty cage. The animal takes in carbon monoxide twenty times as fast as a person, so it collapses long before you feel anything. Feed it grain from the other hand at least every three days.
tfcpp.info.settling_baffle: Place these in a closed chamber that furnace fumes pass through. Arsenic, antimony and zinc oxide dust settles on the plates, and is scraped off by right-clicking with an empty hand. Scraping stirs up some of the dust, so do not breathe it.
tfcpp.info.shaft_load: Every machine on a shaft takes torque from its source. The more it has to drive, the slower it turns, and past what the source can start against it stops. A water wheel gives its best power at half of its free speed. Pumps take more torque the higher they lift. Water itself no longer multiplies, and a pump moves it from its intake to its outlet.
tfcpp.info.sulfur_burner: A trough of fire clay in a pipe, where powdered sulfur burns in the air of the pipe to sulfur dioxide, which the lead chamber takes up. It lights from the hot flue and needs oxygen: with too little, the sulfur only smoulders. Sulfur dioxide chokes, so the trough must stand in a pipe that carries the gas away.
tfcpp.info.thomas_slag: Basic slag from a converter on a dolomite lining, full of calcium phosphate. Grind it in a quern for a phosphorus fertiliser.
